home.title: Welcome to onboarding
home.subtitle: Find your department's roadmap, work through each step, and track your progress as you ramp up.

sidebar.defaultDescription: Select any step to see details here. Dashed nodes are optional — hover any node to trace its dependency chain.
sidebar.skillIntro: One of the skills you'll build while working through

coming-soon.label: Coming soon
coming-soon.description:
This role's onboarding roadmap hasn't been published yet — check back soon.

We're actively building out the step-by-step path for this role, the same way we did for DBAs, developers, and support. In the meantime, ping your onboarding contact — they can tell you what's available right now and roughly when the rest is landing.

dba-tools-setup.label: Tools Setup
dba-tools-setup.description:
Install SSMS, Azure Data Studio, and set up your editor before anything else on this roadmap.

You'll live in SSMS for day-to-day SQL Server work and reach for Azure Data Studio when you're on a Mac or want a lighter, cross-platform editor for Azure SQL. Getting both installed and connected now means the AZ-900 and DP-900 labs later don't stall on a missing tool.

ms-learn-setup.label: Microsoft Learn Setup
ms-learn-setup.description:
Create a personal Microsoft account to track your training progress and badges.

This is step zero — everything else in this roadmap, from AZ-900 onward, hangs off this one account. It takes five minutes and means your certificates and progress actually stick around after you earn them.

az-900.label: AZ-900 · Azure Fundamentals
az-900.description:
Introduction to cloud concepts and core Azure services.

Every cloud role starts here, DBAs included — you can't administer a database in the cloud without first understanding what the cloud actually is. Expect terms like IaaS, PaaS, and availability zones to feel fuzzy at first; that's normal, and it clears up fast once DP-900 gets more concrete.

dp-900.label: DP-900 · Azure Data Fundamentals
dp-900.description:
Basics of databases, SQL/NoSQL, and data workloads.

This is where AZ-900's general cloud knowledge narrows in on data specifically — relational vs. non-relational, and the Azure services built for each. It's the last stop before you start writing actual T-SQL, so the vocabulary you pick up here will show up constantly in the next step.

tsql-fundamentals.label: T-SQL Fundamentals
tsql-fundamentals.description:
Write and tune real queries: joins, indexes, stored procedures, and the basics of query performance.

This is the hands-on skill you'll use every single day as a DBA, way more than any certification. Think slow-query tickets where you have to figure out why a join is scanning the whole table instead of using an index — that instinct gets built right here, and it's exactly what DP-300 assumes you already have.

dp-300.label: DP-300 · Administering Azure SQL
dp-300.description:
Practical DBA topics: performance, security, backups, maintenance, HADR.

This is the certification that pulls together everything before it — T-SQL, security, and cloud fundamentals — into the actual job of running a production database. Once this clicks, you're ready for the hands-on labs where you'll practice restoring backups and handling failover for real.

intro-videos.label: Internal Intro Videos
intro-videos.description:
Company-specific introduction videos and onboarding contacts.

This one's optional and runs alongside your certification path rather than blocking it — think of it as context, not coursework. Watch it whenever you need a break from Microsoft Learn, so you know who to ask when something company-specific comes up.

video-platforms.label: Video Training Platforms
video-platforms.description:
Supplementary courses on Pluralsight, Udemy, and internal Operations recordings.

Also optional — use these if DP-300 left a topic feeling shaky, or if you just learn better from video than from reading docs. There's no expectation to plow through every course; dip in for whatever's still fuzzy before you move into hands-on labs.

hands-on.label: Hands-On Environment
hands-on.description:
A dedicated Azure subscription plus local tools (SQL Server, SSMS) for real DBA labs.

This is where the certifications stop being theory — you get your own sandbox to restore backups, tune slow queries, and set up maintenance jobs without any risk to production. Expect the first couple of labs to take longer than you'd guess; that's just what learning a new environment feels like, and it's exactly what preps you for your first support rotation.

first-rotation.label: First Support Rotation
first-rotation.description:
Shadow a senior DBA, pick up your first tickets, and start building the instincts that only come from real production work.

This is the payoff for everything before it — the certifications and lab time turn into judgment when there's a real ticket and a real person waiting on an answer. You're not on your own here: a senior DBA is right beside you until the instincts kick in on their own.

tools-setup.label: Tools Setup
tools-setup.description:
Install the Azure CLI, your editor, and kubectl before touching any cloud resources.

The Portal is fine for a first look, but almost everything you'll actually do — scripting a deployment, checking a resource's state, debugging a pipeline — goes through the CLI or kubectl instead. Setting these up now, with your editor's Azure/Kubernetes extensions installed, means the IaC and container topics later are hands-on from the first exercise.

cloud-fundamentals.label: Cloud Fundamentals (AZ-900)
cloud-fundamentals.description:
Core cloud concepts and Azure services — the same starting point every cloud role builds on.

AZ-900 gives you the shared vocabulary — IaaS vs. PaaS, regions, availability zones — that every later topic assumes you already have. Once it clicks, networking is where things stop being abstract and start being actual virtual networks you can draw on a whiteboard.

networking.label: Networking & Connectivity
networking.description:
Design and troubleshoot the plumbing that connects everything: virtual networks, gateways, and DNS.

Most "it's broken" tickets in cloud environments trace back to networking — a misconfigured NSG rule, a DNS record pointing at the wrong place. Get comfortable here and compute & storage will make a lot more sense, since every VM and disk you spin up next needs a network to sit on.

compute-storage.label: Compute & Storage
compute-storage.description:
Provision and scale the building blocks of any cloud workload: VMs, disks, and object storage.

This is the part that feels most like "real" cloud engineering — spinning up a VM, sizing a disk, deciding where files actually live. From here the path splits: security fundamentals locks down what you just built, while IaC teaches you to build it without clicking through the portal again.

security-fundamentals.label: Security Fundamentals
security-fundamentals.description:
Lock things down: identity, access control, and secrets management.

This one's optional but worth the detour — a compute resource with no access controls is basically an open door. Think role assignments, managed identities, and keeping secrets out of config files where anyone can read them.

iac.label: Infrastructure as Code
iac.description:
Stop clicking around the portal — define infrastructure in code so it's repeatable and reviewable.

Once your infrastructure lives in a Bicep or Terraform file instead of your click history, someone else can review it, roll it back, and reuse it for the next environment. It's also what makes containers and CI/CD actually practical — you can't automate deployments of infrastructure you can't describe as code.

containers.label: Containers & Kubernetes
containers.description:
Package and orchestrate workloads with Docker and Azure Kubernetes Service.

Containers solve the "works on my machine" problem by packaging an app with everything it needs to run anywhere. Once you're comfortable building images, CI/CD is the natural next step — that's how those images actually get built and shipped automatically instead of by hand.

cicd.label: CI/CD & Automation
cicd.description:
Automate builds, tests, and deployments so shipping code is boring — in a good way.

A good pipeline means deployments happen the same way every time, at 2pm or 2am, without someone remembering the seventeen manual steps. Once that's humming, monitoring & cost management is what tells you whether what you just shipped is actually behaving — and what it's costing you.

monitoring-cost.label: Monitoring & Cost Management
monitoring-cost.description:
Know what's running, what it costs, and get alerted before something breaks.

This is the difference between finding out about an outage from a customer versus from an alert — and finding out about a cost spike from finance versus from a dashboard. It ties together everything you've built so far, which makes it good prep for pulling it all together in AZ-104.

az-104.label: AZ-104 · Azure Administrator
az-104.description:
The certification that ties it all together: governance, identity, and day-to-day Azure administration.

By this point you've touched networking, compute, containers, and monitoring hands-on — AZ-104 is where that practical experience gets organized into the official administrator skill set. Passing it is a solid signal you're ready to own real Azure environments, not just poke at a sandbox.

company-tools-setup.label: Company Tools & Systems
company-tools-setup.description:
Get every account, channel, and system dialed in before day one is even over.

This is the boring-but-essential setup that everything else depends on — you can't triage an incident in a ticketing system you can't log into. Once you're set up, ITSM basics is where you learn how those tools actually get used day to day.

itsm-basics.label: IT Service Management Basics
itsm-basics.description:
Learn how requests, incidents, and changes flow through the organization — and why the process exists.

The process can feel like red tape until you see it prevent a bad change from taking down production — then it clicks. This is also the map you'll use constantly once you're actually handling incidents in the next step.

incident-management.label: Incident Management
incident-management.description:
When something breaks, know how to triage it, escalate it, and write it up afterward.

This is the core of the job — everything before it was preparation for exactly this moment. From here the path splits: scripting for the repetitive parts of the fix, and monitoring so you catch the next one before a customer does.

monitoring-alerting.label: Monitoring & Alerting
monitoring-alerting.description:
Read dashboards fluently and know what an alert is actually telling you to do.

An alert that fires at 3am is only useful if you can tell in ten seconds whether it's urgent or noise. Getting fluent here feeds straight into documentation — the runbooks you write next are what make an alert actionable instead of just alarming.

scripting-automation.label: Scripting & Automation Basics
scripting-automation.description:
Turn repetitive manual work into a script — your future self will thank you.

This one's optional but pays off fast: the third time you do the same five manual steps during an incident is usually the moment to automate them. Even a rough script beats retyping the same commands under pressure.

documentation.label: Documentation & Runbooks
documentation.description:
If it's not written down, it didn't happen. Build the habit of documenting as you go.

A good runbook means the next person to hit this incident — maybe you, six months from now — doesn't have to re-solve it from scratch. It's also what turns communication & escalation from guesswork into something you can point people at.

communication-escalation.label: Communication & Escalation
communication-escalation.description:
Say the right thing to the right person at the right time — especially when things are on fire.

A calm, clear status update during an outage does more for trust than a fast fix with no communication. Once an incident is actually resolved, continuous improvement is where you look back and make sure it doesn't repeat.

continuous-improvement.label: Continuous Improvement
continuous-improvement.description:
Look back at what happened, find the pattern, and make the process better next time.

This closes the loop on everything else in the roadmap — a postmortem that just says "fixed it" wastes the one useful thing an incident gives you: a chance to prevent the next one. Look for the pattern behind three similar tickets and you've usually found a process fix worth making.

support-tools-setup.label: Support Tools Setup
support-tools-setup.description:
Get your helpdesk software, ticketing system, and knowledge base ready before the first ticket lands.

This is the setup that makes everything after it possible — you can't practice customer communication in a helpdesk tool you haven't logged into yet. Get it dialed in now so nothing's in the way once real tickets start showing up.

customer-communication.label: Customer Communication Basics
customer-communication.description:
Learn to write and speak in a way that calms people down instead of winding them up.

A frustrated customer usually just wants to feel heard before they want a fix — tone matters as much as the actual answer. This is the foundation for triage next: how you say something and how fast you sort it are two halves of the same skill.

ticket-triage-support.label: Ticket Triage & Prioritization
ticket-triage-support.description:
Figure out what's urgent, what can wait, and who else needs to know.

Good triage is what keeps a busy queue from feeling chaotic — a P1 outage and a "how do I change my password" ticket need very different responses, and knowing which is which fast is the job. Once you can sort tickets confidently, product knowledge is what lets you actually answer them.

product-knowledge-support.label: Product Knowledge for Support
product-knowledge-support.description:
Build a mental map of the product so you can answer the top questions from memory.

Most tickets repeat the same handful of questions — once you know the product cold, you're answering from memory instead of searching docs mid-conversation. That same familiarity is exactly what you'll lean on next when troubleshooting takes you past the FAQ.

troubleshooting-diagnostics.label: Troubleshooting & Diagnostics
troubleshooting-diagnostics.description:
Go beyond the FAQ — read logs, reproduce bugs, and track down the actual root cause.

This is where support starts to feel like detective work: reproducing a bug a customer described in three vague sentences, then pinning down why it happens. When you genuinely can't crack it, escalation & collaboration is how you hand it off without losing everything you've already dug up.

escalation-collaboration.label: Escalation & Cross-Team Collaboration
escalation-collaboration.description:
Know when to hand a ticket off to engineering, and how to do it without losing context.

A bad handoff means engineering re-asks the customer everything you already found out; a good one includes logs, repro steps, and what you've ruled out. Get comfortable with that, and customer satisfaction metrics are where you see whether your work is actually landing well with customers.

customer-satisfaction.label: Customer Satisfaction & Metrics
customer-satisfaction.description:
Understand what CSAT and response-time targets actually measure — and how your work moves them.

These numbers aren't just for reporting upward — a dip in CSAT after a fast-but-curt reply is a real signal about tone, not just speed. Once you can read your own metrics, you're ready for a first solo shift and can tell for yourself how it's going.

first-solo-shift.label: First Solo Shift
first-solo-shift.description:
Handle your own ticket queue with a safety net one review away.

This is everything before it, put together for real — your own queue, your own calls on triage and tone, with someone still checking your work before it ships. It's the last step before support becomes just what you do, not what you're learning.

tools-setup.label: Tools Setup
tools-setup.description:
Get your editor, Postman, and browser DevTools set up before you write your first test case.

You don't need to code to be a strong QA engineer, but you do need to poke at requests in Postman and read a network tab in DevTools without help. Both take five minutes to install and will save you from ever having to say "can someone check this API for me?"

qa-fundamentals.label: QA Fundamentals
qa-fundamentals.description:
Understand where testing fits in the software lifecycle and why bugs are cheaper to catch early.

A bug caught before it ships costs a comment on a ticket; the same bug in production costs a customer, a hotfix, and everyone's afternoon. Once that framing sticks, manual testing is where you start actually finding those bugs yourself.

manual-testing.label: Manual Testing
manual-testing.description:
Write test plans, explore the product like a curious user, and report what you find clearly.

This is where you build the instinct for "what happens if I do this weird thing" that no automated script has yet. Every bug you find here needs to go somewhere useful — that's exactly what bug tracking is for.

bug-tracking.label: Bug Tracking & Triage
bug-tracking.description:
File bugs that developers can actually act on — clear steps, clear severity, no guesswork.

A bug report that just says "it's broken" sends a developer on a scavenger hunt; one with exact repro steps and severity gets fixed same-day. From here the path splits: API testing digs into the layer users never see, while automation turns your best reports into repeatable checks.

api-testing.label: API Testing
api-testing.description:
Test the layer users never see: requests, responses, status codes, and edge cases.

A lot of the nastiest bugs live below the UI — a 500 error the frontend quietly swallows, or a field that's required in the docs but not actually enforced. Once you're comfortable poking at endpoints directly, performance testing is the natural next question: does it still work when a thousand people hit it at once?

automation-fundamentals.label: Automation Fundamentals
automation-fundamentals.description:
Turn your best manual tests into scripts that run themselves, every time.

This is optional but changes the math on your time — the login-and-checkout flow you've clicked through fifty times is exactly what a script should be doing instead of you. Get a handful of these running and CI/CD for QA is where they start earning their keep automatically.

performance-testing.label: Performance & Load Testing
performance-testing.description:
Find out how the system behaves under real pressure, before your users do.

This one's optional but eye-opening the first time — a feature that feels instant with five users can crawl or fall over at five thousand. It's also a strong complement to CI/CD for QA, since load issues are exactly the kind of thing you want caught before a release, not after.

cicd-for-qa.label: CI/CD & Test Pipelines
cicd-for-qa.description:
Wire your tests into the pipeline so broken code gets caught before it ships.

Once tests run automatically on every pull request, a broken build blocks itself instead of relying on someone remembering to run the suite. That's the safety net you'll be leaning on for your first QA rotation, where you're covering a real release.

first-qa-rotation.label: First QA Rotation
first-qa-rotation.description:
Own test coverage for a real release, alongside a mentor who's done it before.

This is where manual testing, bug reports, and automation stop being separate skills and become one job: deciding what needs coverage for an actual release going out the door. A mentor is there to sanity-check your calls, but the coverage plan is yours.

dev-environment-setup.label: Dev Environment Setup
dev-environment-setup.description:
Get Git, your editor, and local tooling configured so you can actually start writing code.

A clean setup now saves you from fighting your tools later instead of the actual problem. Once this is sorted, programming fundamentals is where the real learning starts.

programming-fundamentals.label: Programming Fundamentals
programming-fundamentals.description:
The building blocks that don't change no matter what language or framework you land on.

Loops, conditionals, functions, data structures — learn to think in these and switching languages later becomes a syntax problem, not a relearning-everything problem. Web fundamentals is where you'll immediately put this thinking to use, just aimed at the browser.

web-fundamentals.label: Web Fundamentals
web-fundamentals.description:
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — how a page actually gets built and behaves in a browser.

This is the layer users actually see and click on, so bugs here are the ones people notice first. Once a page can display and react to clicks on its own, backend basics is where you learn what's actually happening behind that click.

backend-basics.label: Backend Basics
backend-basics.description:
APIs, databases, and authentication — the parts of an app users never see but always depend on.

This is where "click a button" turns into "save a row in a database and remember who you are next time." From here the path splits: testing & code quality for making sure this stuff keeps working, and version control workflows for collaborating on it with other people.

testing-code-quality.label: Testing & Code Quality
testing-code-quality.description:
Write code that's easy to trust: tests, reviews, and a linter that has your back.

This one's optional but pays for itself the first time a test catches a bug before a reviewer has to. It sets you up well for version control workflows, since a PR with passing tests is a much easier sell to a reviewer.

version-control-workflows.label: Version Control Workflows
version-control-workflows.description:
Branch, open a pull request, and survive your first merge conflict without panicking.

Everyone hits their first ugly merge conflict — the trick is learning to read the diff calmly instead of panicking and force-pushing over someone's work. Once branching and PRs feel routine, CI/CD & deployment is what actually happens to your code after it's merged.

cicd-deployment.label: CI/CD & Deployment
cicd-deployment.description:
Understand how code goes from your laptop to production — and how to roll it back if it doesn't.

Knowing there's a rollback button is what makes shipping less scary — you don't need every deploy to be perfect, just recoverable. That confidence is exactly what carries you into your first feature ship, where all of this comes together on a real ticket.

first-feature-ship.label: First Feature Shipped
first-feature-ship.description:
Take a real ticket from breakdown to production, with a pair and a reviewer alongside you.

This is everything before it, end to end, on a ticket that actually matters — breaking down the work, writing the code, getting it reviewed, and watching it deploy. Having a pair alongside you means the first time doesn't have to be perfect, just done.

tools-setup.label: Tools Setup
tools-setup.description:
Get logged into the CRM, your dialer, and the rest of the sales stack before your first call.

Nothing here is complicated, but a rep who's still figuring out how to log a call in week two is a rep who's losing pipeline data every single day before that. Getting this set up on day one means CRM fundamentals next is about using the tool well, not discovering where the buttons are.

product-onboarding.label: Product & Company Onboarding
product-onboarding.description:
Learn what we sell, who we sell it to, and why they should care.

You can't sell what you don't understand, and prospects can tell within thirty seconds whether you actually know the product. Once this is solid, CRM fundamentals is where you start tracking the people you'll be having these conversations with.

crm-fundamentals.label: CRM Fundamentals
crm-fundamentals.description:
Keep your pipeline clean — the CRM only helps if the data in it is trustworthy.

A stale CRM means you're guessing who to follow up with instead of knowing; a clean one tells you exactly who's gone quiet and who's ready for a next step. That discipline is what makes prospecting actually work, since it's the same pipeline you'll be filling.

prospecting.label: Prospecting & Lead Generation
prospecting.description:
Find the right people to talk to before you ever pick up the phone.

A call to the wrong person wastes both your time and theirs — good prospecting means you already know why this account is worth calling before you dial. Get that right and sales calls & demos become about the conversation itself, not about justifying why you're there.

sales-calls-demos.label: Sales Calls & Demos
sales-calls-demos.description:
Run a discovery call and a demo that actually answers 'why should I care?'

A demo that shows every feature answers nothing; one built around what this specific prospect just told you they need is what actually lands. From here the path splits: negotiation for closing the deal, and account management for what happens once they're a customer.

negotiation-closing.label: Negotiation & Closing
negotiation-closing.description:
Handle pricing pushback and objections without giving away the deal.

This is optional but sharpens a real skill: the instinct to hold a price while still making the prospect feel heard, instead of jumping straight to a discount. It pairs well with account management, since the terms you agree to now are what you'll be living with for the life of the account.

account-management.label: Account Management
account-management.description:
What happens after the deal closes: renewals, handoffs, and keeping customers happy.

Closing the deal is only half the job — a customer who churns at renewal because no one checked in erases the win. Understanding this side of the relationship is exactly what sales metrics measure next: retention and expansion, not just new logos.

sales-metrics.label: Sales Metrics & Reporting
sales-metrics.description:
Understand the numbers that define whether a quarter went well — and why.

Quota, conversion rate, average deal size — these aren't just for the sales dashboard, they tell you where your own process is leaking deals. Once you can read them, your first deal closed is where you finally see your own numbers move for a real reason.

first-deal-closed.label: First Deal Closed
first-deal-closed.description:
Run a real deal start to finish, with a mentor checking in along the way.

This is everything before it in one deal — prospecting, the calls, the negotiation, and the close — done for real instead of practiced in pieces. A mentor checking in means you get to make the calls yourself while still having someone to catch a mistake before it costs the deal.
